Fine structures are semantic inspection anchors and must be recalibrated against any enabled production GLB. Atlas V4 intentionally routes microscopic structures to their owning system pages until dedicated child routes exist.

hotspots.label: Root system
hotspots.detail: Primary, lateral & fine absorbing roots
hotspots.copy: Primary and lateral roots branch into fine absorbing roots that anchor the plant, acquire water and ions, respire, and interact with the rhizosphere.

hotspots.label: Root tips
hotspots.detail: Apical growth and young absorption zones
hotspots.copy: Young root tips contain the root apical meristem and newly differentiating tissues. Just behind the tip, young root surfaces are especially important for water and mineral acquisition.

hotspots.label: Stem & vascular system
hotspots.detail: Main stem, branches, xylem & phloem pathway
hotspots.copy: The main stem and branches form a continuous vascular skeleton. Xylem moves water and minerals; phloem redistributes sugars and other assimilates among sources and sinks.

hotspots.label: Nodes & branching
hotspots.detail: Axillary sites and branch junctions
hotspots.copy: Nodes carry leaves, branches, and axillary meristems. Their spacing and bud activity reveal how developmental signaling and environment shape plant architecture.

hotspots.label: Shoot apex
hotspots.detail: Apical meristem and newest growth
hotspots.copy: The shoot apex contains actively dividing meristematic tissue that produces new stem, leaf, and later reproductive structures. Its activity strongly influences vertical growth and branching patterns.

hotspots.label: Fan leaves
hotspots.detail: Serrated leaflets, petioles, blades & veins
hotspots.copy: Fan leaves are major photosynthetic organs. Their blades capture light while stomata regulate gas exchange and transpiration, and petioles connect each leaf to the vascular system.

hotspots.label: Petiole
hotspots.detail: Leaf stalk connecting blade to stem
hotspots.copy: The petiole positions the leaf blade and contains vascular bundles that connect leaf tissues with the stem. Its angle and mechanical state also change with water status and development.

hotspots.label: Leaf venation
hotspots.detail: Midrib and lateral vascular network
hotspots.copy: The midrib and lateral veins distribute water and minerals into the blade and export photosynthates through phloem. Venation also provides mechanical support across the thin leaf surface.

hotspots.label: Flowers & inflorescences
hotspots.detail: Female floral clusters, bracts & sugar leaves
hotspots.copy: Female inflorescences contain densely packed floral structures, subtending bracts, sugar leaves, stigmas, and resinous surfaces that change substantially through maturation.

hotspots.label: Bracts
hotspots.detail: Protective floral structures surrounding ovules
hotspots.copy: Bracts are small leaf-like floral structures associated with the female flower. They surround reproductive tissues and are among the most conspicuously resinous tissues of the inflorescence.

hotspots.label: Sugar leaves
hotspots.detail: Small resinous leaves within flower clusters
hotspots.copy: Sugar leaves are small leaves embedded within and around the inflorescence. They contribute photosynthesis locally and frequently carry abundant glandular trichomes.

hotspots.label: Reproductive structures
hotspots.detail: Female flowers, preflowers & pollen-reception surfaces
hotspots.copy: Female reproductive structures connect visible flower anatomy to sex expression, pollen reception, fertilization, embryo development, and seed formation.

hotspots.label: Stigmas
hotspots.detail: Pollen-receptive floral structures
hotspots.copy: Paired stigmas emerge from each pistillate flower and participate in pollen capture. Their appearance changes with flower age, pollination status, and environmental exposure.

hotspots.label: Glandular trichomes
hotspots.detail: Stalks and secretory gland heads
hotspots.copy: Glandular trichomes include stalks, secretory disc cells, and gland heads. Their form and density vary by tissue, developmental stage, genotype, and environmental conditions.

hotspots.label: Root crown
hotspots.detail: Transition between stem base and root system
hotspots.copy: The root crown is the transition zone where the shoot base meets the root system. It carries vascular continuity between above-ground organs and the major structural roots.

hotspots.label: Lateral roots
hotspots.detail: Branching structural and absorbing roots
hotspots.copy: Lateral roots branch from older root axes and expand the volume of substrate explored by the plant. Their younger branches contribute strongly to water and mineral acquisition.

hotspots.label: Fine absorbing roots
hotspots.detail: Young small-diameter roots at the active root frontier
hotspots.copy: Fine roots provide much of the actively absorbing root surface. Their abundance, age, oxygen supply, and rhizosphere conditions strongly affect water and ion uptake.

hotspots.label: Internodes
hotspots.detail: Stem segments between successive nodes
hotspots.copy: Internodes are stem segments between nodes. Their length integrates genetics, light environment, temperature, hormones, developmental stage, and competition within the canopy.

hotspots.label: Axillary buds
hotspots.detail: Meristematic buds formed in leaf axils
hotspots.copy: Axillary buds form where leaves meet the stem. Their dormancy or outgrowth controls much of the plant's branching architecture and responds to apical dominance and environmental signals.

hotspots.label: Xylem pathway
hotspots.detail: Water-conducting vascular tissue
hotspots.copy: Xylem conducts water and dissolved mineral nutrients upward through the plant and also contributes structural support. Flow depends on root uptake, transpiration, hydraulic continuity, and embolism resistance.

hotspots.label: Phloem pathway
hotspots.detail: Assimilate-conducting vascular tissue
hotspots.copy: Phloem transports sugars and other assimilates from source tissues toward sinks such as growing shoots, roots, flowers, and developing seeds. Direction changes with source-sink relationships.

hotspots.label: Leaflets
hotspots.detail: Individual serrated units of a compound fan leaf
hotspots.copy: Cannabis fan leaves are palmately compound, with multiple serrated leaflets attached around a common point. Leaflet number, size, and shape vary with genetics and developmental conditions.

hotspots.label: Serrated leaf margin
hotspots.detail: Toothed edge of the leaflet blade
hotspots.copy: The serrated margin defines the characteristic toothed outline of many Cannabis leaflets. Margin form is useful descriptively but should not be treated as a stand-alone indicator of cultivar identity or plant health.

hotspots.label: Leaf blade
hotspots.detail: Broad photosynthetic lamina tissue
hotspots.copy: The leaf blade contains photosynthetic mesophyll, vascular networks, epidermal tissues, and stomata. Its orientation, temperature, hydration, and light environment strongly influence gas exchange.

hotspots.label: Stomatal surface
hotspots.detail: Microscopic pores controlling gas exchange
hotspots.copy: Stomata are microscopic epidermal pores controlled by guard cells. They regulate carbon dioxide entry and water-vapor loss, linking photosynthesis to plant water status and vapor-pressure conditions.

hotspots.label: Preflower site
hotspots.detail: Early reproductive structures at mature nodes
hotspots.copy: Preflowers develop at nodes as plants reach reproductive maturity. Their anatomy can reveal sex expression before dense inflorescences form, but timing varies with genotype and environment.

hotspots.label: Pistillate flower
hotspots.detail: Individual female flower within the inflorescence
hotspots.copy: A pistillate Cannabis flower contains the ovary, ovule, style and paired stigmas, with the flower closely enclosed by a resinous bract. Many individual flowers make up the visible inflorescence.

hotspots.label: Ovary & ovule
hotspots.detail: Female reproductive tissues where fertilization and seed development occur
hotspots.copy: Inside the pistillate flower, the ovary contains an ovule. After successful pollination and fertilization, embryo and seed development proceed while surrounding floral tissues mature.

hotspots.label: Inflorescence axis
hotspots.detail: Branching framework supporting clustered flowers
hotspots.copy: The inflorescence axis and short branches support many individual flowers, bracts, and sugar leaves. Their spacing and developmental timing shape the density and architecture of the flowering canopy.

hotspots.label: Capitate-stalked trichomes
hotspots.detail: Prominent glandular trichomes with stalk and secretory head
hotspots.copy: Capitate-stalked glandular trichomes develop a multicellular stalk and enlarged secretory head. They are abundant on mature female floral tissues and contain specialized secretory cells.

hotspots.label: Trichome gland head
hotspots.detail: Secretory head containing specialized disc cells and storage cavity
hotspots.copy: The gland head contains secretory disc cells beneath a cuticular storage cavity. Cannabinoids and many volatile compounds accumulate in this glandular system as the trichome develops.

hotspots.label: Trichome stalk
hotspots.detail: Support structure beneath the glandular head
hotspots.copy: The stalk elevates the glandular head above the epidermis and is anatomically distinct from the secretory disc cells. Stalk and head dimensions vary with trichome type and developmental stage.
